articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Escambia County's $2.1M tourism contract renewed without bid process
articles.dek: County commissioners approved the marketing deal in a consent agenda vote last week. Records show the vendor's CEO donated to three commissioners' campaigns.
brief: Escambia County commissioners renewed a $2.1 million tourism marketing contract with Emerald Coast Media Group without competitive bidding
Campaign finance records show the vendor's CEO contributed $4,500 to three sitting commissioners between 2022 and 2025
The contract appeared on the consent agenda and passed 4-1 with no public discussion
articles.body:
The item appeared on page seven of the consent agenda. No discussion. No questions from the dais. In under three seconds, Escambia County commissioners approved a $2.1 million contract renewal for tourism marketing services.

The May 9 vote extended the county's deal with Emerald Coast Media Group for another three years. The Destin-based firm has held the contract since 2020. This marks the second renewal without a competitive bidding process.

Campaign finance records reviewed by The Flightline show Emerald Coast Media Group CEO Richard Harmon contributed $4,500 to three of the four commissioners who voted to approve the contract. The donations occurred between 2022 and 2025.

The money trail

According to Escambia County Supervisor of Elections records, Harmon gave $2,000 to Commission Chairman Jeff Bergosh's 2024 reelection campaign. He contributed $1,500 to District 3 Commissioner Lumon May in 2022 and $1,000 to District 5 Commissioner Steven Barry in 2023.

All three voted to approve the contract renewal.

District 2 Commissioner Mike Kohler, who did not receive donations from Harmon, cast the lone dissenting vote. District 4 Commissioner Robert Bender, also without recorded donations from Harmon, was absent.

Harmon did not respond to multiple requests for comment. His office referred inquiries to the company's legal counsel, who declined to comment on the record.

No bid, no debate

County purchasing policy allows contract renewals without competitive bidding when the original agreement included renewal options. The 2020 contract with Emerald Coast Media Group contained two three-year renewal clauses.

But the policy also grants commissioners discretion to require new bids at any time. None requested it.

"The vendor has performed satisfactorily," county spokesperson Kimberly Ross wrote in an email to The Flightline. "There was no indication that rebidding was necessary."

Ross said the Tourist Development Council, which advises commissioners on tourism spending, recommended the renewal. TDC meeting minutes from April show the recommendation passed unanimously. The minutes contain no record of discussion about competitive alternatives.

Commissioner Kohler said he voted no because he believes contracts of this size should face regular competition.

"Two million dollars is real money," Kohler said in an interview. "I think taxpayers deserve to know we're getting the best deal. The only way to know that is to let other firms compete."

Kohler said he raised concerns about the bidding process in a pre-meeting briefing but was told the renewal complied with county policy.

What the contract covers

The $2.1 million agreement funds digital advertising, social media management, video production and media buying for Visit Pensacola, the county's tourism marketing arm. Bed tax revenues—not general fund dollars—pay for the contract.

Emerald Coast Media Group produces promotional content highlighting Pensacola Beach, the National Naval Aviation Museum and downtown attractions. The company also manages paid campaigns targeting drive-market tourists in Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi.

Tourism officials point to record visitor numbers as evidence the marketing works. Escambia County welcomed 4.2 million visitors in 2025, according to Visit Pensacola data, up from 3.8 million in 2020 when the contract began.

Whether those gains resulted from the marketing campaign or broader post-pandemic travel trends is unclear. Comparable Florida Gulf Coast destinations saw similar increases during the same period.

Commission responds

Chairman Bergosh defended the contract and rejected any suggestion that campaign contributions influenced his vote.

"I don't even know who gives to my campaign half the time," Bergosh said. "My treasurer handles that. I vote based on what's best for the county."

Bergosh said Emerald Coast Media Group earned the renewal through consistent performance. He noted that no other vendors contacted the county to express interest in the work.

"If someone wanted to compete, they could have reached out," he said. "No one did."

Commissioner May did not respond to interview requests. Commissioner Barry's office said he was unavailable but provided a written statement calling the contract "a good value for tourism promotion."

Legal but questions remain

Nothing in the public record suggests the contract or the campaign contributions violated Florida law. State ethics rules prohibit quid pro quo arrangements but do not bar vendors from donating to elected officials who oversee their contracts.

Government watchdog groups say the optics matter even when conduct is legal.

"This is exactly the kind of thing that erodes public trust," said Ben Wilcox, research director at Integrity Florida, a nonpartisan ethics organization. "When the same people giving you campaign money are getting multimillion-dollar contracts without competition, voters are right to ask questions."

Wilcox said the lack of discussion before the vote compounds the perception problem.

"Consent agendas exist for routine business," he said. "A $2 million contract with a campaign donor isn't routine. It deserved a public conversation."

The renewed contract runs through May 2029. It includes one additional three-year renewal option, which commissioners could approve without bidding under current policy.

articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Pensacola Beach parking lot sale stalls as lease questions surface
articles.dek: The proposed sale of the Casino Beach lot has exposed a 40-year-old dispute over who actually controls the land beneath it.
brief: Escambia County's planned $8.2 million sale of the Casino Beach parking lot to a private developer has been delayed after Santa Rosa Island Authority board members raised questions about existing lease agreements dating to 1984.
The dispute centers on whether the county can sell land that may still be subject to a 99-year ground lease held by the SRIA, a quasi-governmental body that manages development on the barrier island.
County attorneys and SRIA counsel have scheduled a joint review of the original lease documents, pushing any potential sale into late 2026 at the earliest.
articles.body:
The asphalt stretches flat and unremarkable from the Gulfside Pavilion to the edge of Via de Luna Drive. Three hundred parking spaces. A few palm trees. Nothing about the Casino Beach lot suggests it could upend forty years of assumed authority over Pensacola Beach.

But that's where things stand.

Escambia County's Board of County Commissioners announced in March it had received an unsolicited offer from Gulf Coast Development Partners LLC to purchase the lot for $8.2 million. The Jacksonville-based firm proposed a mixed-use project: ground-floor retail, vacation rentals above, structured parking to replace the surface spaces.

The commission voted 4-1 on March 12 to begin negotiations. Commissioner Jeff Bergosh cast the lone dissent, citing concerns about public beach access.

Then the Santa Rosa Island Authority got involved.

At its April 23 meeting, the SRIA board heard from its executive director, Paolo Ghio, who told members he had discovered what he called "significant ambiguity" in the chain of title for the Casino Beach lot.

"We've operated under the assumption that the county owns this property outright," Ghio said during the meeting. "That assumption may be incorrect."

The issue traces to 1984, when the SRIA entered into a 99-year ground lease with Escambia County for several parcels along the beach's commercial core. The lease, recorded with the Escambia County Clerk of Court, granted the SRIA development and management rights while the county retained fee simple ownership.

But the Casino Beach lot's status is murky. A 1986 amendment to the original lease appears to exclude the parking lot from SRIA control. A 1991 memo from the county attorney's office suggests otherwise.

"We have two documents that say two different things," SRIA board chair Brigette Brooks said in an interview. "Until we know which one governs, we can't tell the county what they can or can't do with this land."

The stakes extend beyond one parking lot.

If the 1984 ground lease does cover the Casino Beach parcel, the county would need SRIA approval for any sale—and the SRIA would retain authority over what gets built there. If the 1986 amendment controls, the county can proceed without the authority's consent.

The question matters because the SRIA and county have clashed before over development standards, density, and public access requirements. The authority has historically taken a more restrictive approach to commercial development on the island than the county commission.

"This isn't about blocking progress," Brooks said. "It's about making sure whoever develops this property follows the same rules everyone else on the beach follows."

County Commissioner Doug Underhill, who voted for negotiations in March, declined to comment on the lease dispute. A spokesperson for the county administrator's office said only that "the county is confident in its legal position" and that "all appropriate due diligence will be conducted before any sale is finalized."

Gulf Coast Development Partners has not withdrawn its offer. A representative for the firm, reached by phone, said the company is "monitoring the situation" and remains interested in the project.

The firm's principal, Marcus Whitley, has developed hotel and condo properties in Panama City Beach, Destin, and Orange Beach, Alabama. Public records show no previous projects in Escambia or Santa Rosa counties.

The SRIA and county attorney's office have scheduled a joint document review for June 3. Ghio said he expects the process to take several months.

"These are old records," he said. "Some of them aren't digitized. Some of them may not exist anymore. We have to be thorough."

In the meantime, the Casino Beach lot remains what it has been for decades: a place to park your car before you walk to the water. Three hundred spaces. A few palm trees. And a question nobody thought to ask until someone offered to buy it.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Blue Angels homecoming week brings 200,000 visitors and a housing crisis for performers
articles.dek: With the July show three weeks out, visiting pilots and crew are competing with tourists for the same sold-out hotel rooms.
brief: The July 11-12 Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show is expected to draw over 200,000 spectators to NAS Pensacola, but visiting demonstration teams face a new problem: nowhere to stay.
Hotel rooms across Escambia and Santa Rosa counties are already 94% booked for show week, with remaining inventory priced at $400-$800 per night.
Navy officials are exploring emergency housing options including barracks space and a partnership with Airbnb hosts willing to offer military rates.
articles.body:
The woman behind the front desk at the Hampton Inn on Airport Boulevard doesn't need to check her computer anymore. She's memorized the answer.

"July 10th through 13th? Sold out. Have been since February."

Three weeks before the Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show, Pensacola's hotel rooms have vanished. The 200,000 spectators expected to crowd NAS Pensacola on July 11 and 12 started booking months ago. What nobody planned for: the pilots and crew from visiting demonstration teams need those same rooms.

And they can't get them.

A logistical puzzle with no obvious solution

The Homecoming show isn't just the Blue Angels. The Canadian Forces Snowbirds are coming. So is the F-22 Raptor Demo Team, the Army Golden Knights parachute team, and civilian aerobatic performers. Combined, that's roughly 180 pilots, crew chiefs, mechanics and support personnel who need housing for four to six nights.

"We've always handled billeting through normal channels," said Lt. Cmdr. Patricia Vargas, public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Pensacola. "Block reservations at partner hotels, some barracks space for overflow. This year, those blocks filled with tourists before we could confirm them."

The problem is timing. Homecoming show dates are set 18 months in advance. Hotel contracts typically finalize eight to ten months out. But Pensacola's tourism surge—Visit Pensacola reported a 23% increase in summer bookings over 2025—has compressed that window. Revenue management systems at major hotel chains now release rooms to the highest bidder in real time.

"The Navy rate is $129 a night," Vargas said. "Those rooms are selling for $500."

The numbers don't work

A Flightline analysis of booking data from Hotels.com, Expedia and direct hotel inventory found 847 available rooms across Escambia and Santa Rosa counties for the nights of July 10-12. That's out of an estimated 14,200 total rooms—a 94% occupancy rate before the show even starts.

Of those 847 rooms, only 12 were priced below $300 per night. The median price: $479.

For a crew chief making E-5 pay, that's a week's take-home.

"We're not asking for luxury," said Master Sgt. David Okonkwo, a loadmaster with the C-17 West Coast Demo Team who performed at Homecoming in 2023. "We need a bed, a shower and somewhere to store gear. Last time I was here, we stayed at that Fairfield Inn by the mall. Thirty guys, no problems."

That Fairfield Inn is now quoting $612 per night for show week.

Barracks, Airbnb and a scramble for solutions

NAS Pensacola has barracks space, but not much of it. The base's Bachelor Enlisted Quarters can accommodate approximately 400 personnel. Current permanent party and transient training needs already consume most of that capacity.

"We're looking at every option," Vargas said. "Temporary cots in gymnasium spaces. Coordinating with Corry Station and Whiting Field for overflow. Nothing is off the table."

The most unconventional proposal came from an unlikely source. Sarah Beth Hendricks, a Pensacola Beach vacation rental owner, posted in a local Facebook group two weeks ago offering her three-bedroom condo to "any Blue Angels support crew" at $100 per night—roughly one-fifth the market rate.

The post got 2,400 shares.

"I've had this place 11 years," Hendricks said. "I've seen what these guys go through. They're not here to party. They're working 16-hour days so my kids can watch jets fly."

Her offer sparked something. Visit Pensacola confirmed it is now coordinating with Airbnb and VRBO hosts willing to offer military rates, creating an informal registry that NAS Pensacola can access. As of Friday, 34 hosts had signed up, offering 89 beds.

It's not enough. But it's a start.

The tourism boom's hidden cost

Pensacola wanted this. For years, the chamber of commerce, the tourism development council and elected officials pushed for exactly this kind of growth. More visitors. More dollars. More national recognition.

They got it.

Visit Pensacola projects $47 million in direct economic impact from Homecoming weekend alone. Hotel tax revenue for July is forecast to exceed $3.2 million, up from $2.1 million in 2022.

"This is a success story," said Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh at last week's board meeting. "We should be celebrating."

But success has externalities. When every room fills with tourists paying premium rates, the infrastructure that makes the show possible—the pilots, the crews, the mechanics—gets squeezed out.

"It's a market efficiency problem," said Dr. Rick Harper, an economist at the University of West Florida who studies regional tourism. "Hotels respond to price signals. The military can't compete with a family from Atlanta willing to pay $600 for a beach view. So you get this paradox where the event's popularity threatens the event itself."

What happens next

The Navy isn't panicking. Not publicly, anyway. Vargas emphasized that "contingency planning is what we do" and expressed confidence that all visiting personnel would have accommodations by show week.

Behind the scenes, the scramble continues. Emails have gone out to retired military families in the area asking about spare rooms. The Blue Angels Association, a nonprofit supporting current and former team members, has offered to subsidize hotel costs for visiting crews if rooms can be found at any price.

And Hendricks keeps getting messages.

"A woman from Cantonment offered her mother-in-law suite," she said. "A guy with a houseboat in Bayou Chico said he'd take four. It's not organized, but people want to help."

The jets will fly. They always do. But the question lingering over this year's Homecoming is whether Pensacola's tourism success has outgrown the community's ability to support it—and whether anyone saw this coming in time to do something about it.

Three weeks out, the answer is still up in the air.
